Child labour is named outright in 14 districts, though child marriage gets more headlines (35 against 12). In the UIDAI/NITI data, the district-level dominant factor for 32 of 35 Karnataka rows is the share of English-medium schools. They look like two answers to one question; they are two views of the same problem.

methods.state: One factor is ranked highest for the whole state; each district's value is its own figure for that factor.
methods.district: A factor is selected for each district on its own; the value is that factor's fitted weight in the analysis, not a raw percentage.

generalClaims: Change in medium of instruction impacts student dropout
Students struggle to understand lessons in an unfamiliar language

connections.title: Two views of one problem
connections.text: The data compares districts by the conditions of their schools and households; the news follows what happens inside particular families. The data's indicators are all school, teacher, inspection, household-amenity and women's-schooling measures, none of them child labour, marriage or migration, so child labour itself can never appear as a data factor: the data shows the conditions around a child, the news what happens to the child. The same deprivation shows up in both: as a low share or a poor facility in the data, and as a child sent to work or married early in the news.

connections.title: English-medium share as a marker of means
connections.text: English-medium share is the district-level factor for 32 of 35 Karnataka rows. Where few schools teach in English, families who can pay move their children to private English-medium schools, and government schools are left with the poorest households: the ones the news describes sending children to work (child labour is named outright in 14 districts).

connections.title: Language and the SSLC exam
connections.text: Students who studied in Kannada can struggle when lessons and papers lean on English. Failing the SSLC exam often ends schooling, and in a family already weighing work or marriage, one failure is enough. Research from elsewhere links a change in the medium of instruction, and lessons in an unfamiliar language, to students dropping out.

connections.title: Household sanitation and girls' exits
connections.text: Household sanitation is the state-level factor for every Karnataka row. Without a toilet at home, adolescent girls face safety and privacy worries, and families respond by keeping daughters home or marrying them early: the girls' exits the news reports in 23 of 30 districts.

connections.title: Where they already meet
connections.text: In Belagavi and Uttara Kannada, the news itself reports the language of instruction as a problem (Belagavi: "Language gap for migrant children"; Uttara Kannada: "Village school closures, falling enrolment").

prescriptive.text: The NITI model's top changes are about school conditions: classrooms in good condition (27), female teachers (10), student furniture (8), functional toilets (8) districts. The news describes household pressures: poverty & child labour and child marriage & girls' exits. They meet in the classroom: a family weighing a child's work or a daughter's marriage looks at what the school offers, and a leaking room, no desk or no woman teacher can tip that choice. Local reports show the classrooms in good condition gap in 22 of the 27 districts where it is a top change.

connections.title: English-medium schools and child marriage & girls' exits
connections.text: Vijayapura has a middling share of English-medium schools (13.0%, rank 20 of 35). The news here reports "Child marriage through mass weddings". Families also tend to pay for English-medium schooling for sons first.
